S067.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
S067.description: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others.

subtypes.Skin Defects: Excessive preoccupation with practically invisible acne, scars, or complexion.
subtypes.Facial Features: Preoccupation with the shape or size of the nose, eyes, or mouth, which appear normal to others.
subtypes.Asymmetry: Excessive obsession with the face or body not being perfectly symmetrical.
subtypes.Muscle Dysmorphia: The belief that one's body is too small or insufficiently muscular despite being normal or muscular.
subtypes.Specific Body Parts: Obsession that specific parts like hair, teeth, or chest are ugly or abnormal.

S068.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
S068.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to appearance concerns.

subtypes.Mirror Checking or Avoidance: Compulsively checking oneself in the mirror frequently or, conversely, avoiding mirrors strictly.
subtypes.Excessive Camouflaging: Spending excessive time and effort to hide perceived flaws using makeup, clothes, hats, or sunglasses.
subtypes.Skin Picking: Picking or manipulating the skin excessively to remove or 'fix' flaws.
subtypes.Reassurance Seeking: Repetitively asking others for confirmation that one's appearance is okay or not strange.
subtypes.Comparing: Constantly comparing one's body parts with those of passersby or celebrities.
subtypes.Seeking Cosmetic Procedures: Repeatedly seeking or receiving plastic surgery or dermatological procedures.

symptom.disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are either not observable or appear minor to others. This preoccupation is typically accompanied by repetitive behaviors or mental acts (such as mirror checking, excessive grooming, camouflaging, or comparing) that are difficult to control and consume significant time. The condition often begins in adolescence or early adulthood and tends to follow a chronic, fluctuating course, frequently causing substantial distress, social avoidance, and occupational impairment. BDD is distinguished from normal appearance concerns and from eating disorders by the intensity of the preoccupation, the degree of functional impairment, and the focus on specific perceived defects rather than primarily on weight or shape.

patient.stressor: As Joann began planning for retirement and attending more church and community events to "fill the time," she found herself increasingly focused on how she appeared in group photos and on the theater stage crew, especially under bright lights. A milestone birthday party thrown by her bridge club included a slideshow of candid pictures, and she spent the following weeks revisiting those images, dwelling on supposed flaws and dreading future gatherings where cameras might be out. Gradually she started turning down dinner invitations, positioning herself at the back of the choir, and insisting on dimmer lighting at her own dinner parties, which her husband and friends interpreted as a sudden and uncharacteristic withdrawal from community life. Her primary care physician referred her to psychiatric care after she broke down during a routine visit, explaining that she was considering giving up choir, theater volunteering, and even her farewell celebration at work because she "couldn't stand" how she looks anymore.
patient.chief_complaint: “I can’t stop obsessing over how terrible I look in photos and at events, and it’s making me want to avoid people altogether.”

S067.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
S067.description: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others.
S067.manifestation: Ever since that birthday slideshow, all I can see in any picture or mirror is how saggy and crooked my face looks under the lights—my jawline, my neck, these deep lines—and I replay those images over and over in my head until I’m sick with embarrassment and convinced everyone else is noticing it too, even though they say they don’t see what I’m talking about.

S068.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
S068.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to appearance concerns.
S068.manifestation: I spend ridiculous amounts of time before church or choir practice standing inches from the bathroom mirror tilting my head, smoothing my skin, changing my hairstyle and glasses, sometimes taking a dozen selfies and zooming in on every little wrinkle or shadow, and then later I’ll corner my husband or my sister to ask, again, if my face looked lopsided or awful in the photos from that night.

add_requirements.functional_impairment: Over the past several months I’ve started skipping choir practices, turning down theater crew shifts, and even considering canceling my retirement party because I feel so ashamed of how I look in front of others, and it’s really shrinking my social world and leaving me isolated at home.
